summary: Sets out requirements for infrastructure, or carrier, ENUM, which uses ENUM (RFC 3761) technology to help networks interconnect for services addressed by telephone numbers, especially voice over IP. It is informational and describes requirements, not a protocol.

eli5.summary: ENUM turns phone numbers into internet addresses. This explains what phone companies need when they use it behind the scenes to connect their networks to each other.

subtitle: How phone companies connect their networks using internet technology.

tldr.problem: Voice service providers need to connect their networks for phone calls, and they want to use internet-based protocols alongside traditional phone network connections.
tldr.mechanism: Infrastructure ENUM uses the ENUM protocol (which maps phone numbers to internet addresses) for carriers to publish how to reach their networks, rather than just for individual end users.
tldr.outcome: This allows providers to interconnect via IP-based protocols in addition to or instead of traditional phone network links.

today: Infrastructure ENUM is still an informational specification describing requirements rather than a fully standardized protocol. Carriers interested in IP-based interconnection of voice services may use these requirements to guide their systems, but implementation approaches vary. The document has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What Infrastructure ENUM Is
sections.content:
Infrastructure ENUM is the use of ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping) technology for carriers to publish connection information for their phone number blocks. ENUM, defined in RFC 3761, normally lets individual phone users map their numbers to internet addresses. Infrastructure ENUM applies the same technology at the carrier level.

The carrier-of-record is the phone company that owns or controls a block of phone numbers. This could be the company that originally got the numbers from regulators, the company the numbers were ported to, or the company chosen by the end user. The carrier publishes where to find their network's entry point so other carriers can deliver calls to them.
sections.eli5: Infrastructure ENUM is like a special phonebook just for phone companies that shows where their network is on the internet.

sections.title: Why Carriers Need It
sections.content:
Historically, phone companies connected through the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) or wireless networks (PLMN). These are traditional telephone infrastructures. But modern voice services increasingly run on the internet.

Infrastructure ENUM in a public tree (like e164.arpa) lets carriers announce all the phone numbers they serve and point to an internet address where calls can reach them. A carrier can do this whether the end user is on the internet, on a private IP network, or still connected to the traditional phone network. Other carriers can query the ENUM records to find the best way to deliver a call.

This gives carriers flexibility: they can peer with each other via IP without needing direct phone line connections, and they can offer services across both old and new technologies.
sections.eli5: Phone companies can now connect to each other over the internet, not just through old phone network cables. Infrastructure ENUM helps them find each other.

sections.title: What Infrastructure ENUM Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC lists eight key requirements. First, carriers must be able to put DNS records for their numbers into a single public namespace, and queries must always get a response (not be silently rejected). Second, the system must support URI records that identify where to send calls.

Third, the system should support IRIS (Internet Registry Information Service) so authorized parties can look up which carrier owns each number block. Fourth, it must not interfere with end users' ability to choose their own registrars for personal ENUM entries.

Fifth, the name servers must be as reliable and fast as the internet root servers. Sixth, the system must protect privacy by preventing discovery of unlisted numbers. Finally, new proposals should minimize changes to RFC 3761, work with both open and closed numbering systems, and maximize compatibility with existing ENUM deployments.
sections.eli5: The system needs to always answer queries, keep things private, be super reliable, and not break anything that already works.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Concerns
sections.content:
The main security issue is privacy: if a carrier registers only the phone numbers it has assigned to customers, someone could discover unlisted or unpublished numbers by comparing ENUM entries to public directories. The RFC recommends that carriers register their entire allocated range—both assigned and unassigned numbers—routed the same way. This way, a number appearing in ENUM reveals no more than dialing it would.

Another concern is identity disclosure in the URIs returned. If a company publishes URIs that reveal customer names or details, the ENUM system could leak private information. Implementers must be careful not to expose unnecessary details.

The RFC notes that infrastructure ENUM involves carriers rather than individuals, so the security model from the original RFC 3761 may need reconsideration. Where a registry can automatically identify which carrier serves a number, registration might be automated without requiring separate registrars.
sections.eli5: The tricky part is making sure bad actors can't figure out which phone numbers are real just by looking at the ENUM records.

sections.title: Status and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
This RFC is informational: it describes requirements, not a working protocol. The actual architecture to meet these requirements would be designed by others and might require IANA actions later. The document was written by AT&T Labs to guide the design of infrastructure ENUM systems.

Key implementation notes include recognizing that the definition of carrier-of-record varies by jurisdiction and is subject to change by national regulators. The system must be flexible enough to work with different regulatory frameworks. Implementations should also consider that the infrastructure ENUM namespace might be different from the end-user ENUM tree and could be privately operated rather than public.
sections.eli5: This document says what needs to happen, but doesn't specify exactly how. Real systems will fill in those details.
